title: SystemVerilog Interview Question Bank
description: Interview preparation from junior to senior staff: data types and operators, arrays, procedural code and scheduling, races and clocking blocks, interfaces and packages, OOP, constrained randomization, functional coverage, interprocess communication, DPI, and testbench methodology. Model answers cite IEEE 1800-2023.

questions.prompt: Why do most verification teams use SystemVerilog rather than plain Verilog or a general-purpose language such as Python or C++? Name the verification features that plain Verilog lacks, and one situation where another language is the better choice.
questions.rubric: Strong: explains the cost-of-late-bugs motivation without inventing figures; lists the verification features (OOP, constrained random, functional coverage, assertions, interfaces/clocking blocks, dynamic structures and IPC, DPI); knows SystemVerilog absorbed Verilog; gives a reasoned case for Python, C++ or formal. Weak: "SystemVerilog is newer" with no features, or quotes precise cost-of-bug numbers as fact.
questions.model_answer:
Why verification needs its own tools. A bug found after tape-out can mean a silicon respin and a schedule slip, so teams spend heavily on finding bugs before tape-out. Industry figures for the cost of a respin vary and are rarely published with sources, so treat any specific number you hear as an estimate. The point for an interview is the trend: the later a bug is found, the more it costs.

What SystemVerilog adds over Verilog (IEEE 1364). Since IEEE 1800-2009 the two are one standard, so one language and one simulator serve both design and verification (§1.3). The verification features Verilog lacked:

- Classes and OOP for reusable, extensible testbench components (Clause 8).

- Constrained-random stimulus with a built-in solver, seeding and random stability (Clause 18).

- Functional coverage: covergroups and `cover property` to measure what was tested (Clause 19, §16.14.3).

- Assertions (SVA) for temporal checks on protocols (Clause 16).

- Interfaces, clocking blocks and program blocks for race-free connection to the DUT (Clauses 14, 24, 25).

- Dynamic data structures and IPC: queues, dynamic and associative arrays, mailboxes, semaphores, events (Clauses 7, 15).

- DPI to call C models and let C call back (Clause 35).

UVM (IEEE 1800.2) is a class library written in SystemVerilog on top of these features.

When another language fits better. Python benches (cocotb, pyuvm) trade simulation speed and built-in constraint and coverage support for faster writing and a large software ecosystem; they suit small blocks, quick bring-up and teams with strong software skills. C or C++ suits reference models and software-driven SoC tests, usually connected through DPI. Formal tools check properties exhaustively without stimulus at all. Many teams mix them: SystemVerilog/UVM for the bench, C++ for golden models, formal for control logic.
follow_ups: Which of these features would you give up first if you had to verify a block in plain Verilog, and how would you compensate?
What does UVM add that SystemVerilog alone does not?
Why can't a synthesizable RTL subset verify itself?
common_mistakes: Quoting a specific respin cost or the "10x per stage" rule as an established fact.
Describing SystemVerilog as only a design language with some test features bolted on.

sources.doc: Cost-of-bug and respin cost figures (industry estimates, not verifiable)

questions.prompt: Explain `logic`, `wire` and `reg`. Which of the declarations below compile, and when must you use a net such as `wire` instead of `logic`?
questions.rubric: Strong: variable vs net as the real distinction; the single-continuous-driver rule (§6.5); predicts (1) error, (2) legal with resolution, (3) error with the always_comb restriction; states the input-net/output-variable port default (§23.2.2.3); `reg` == `logic`. Weak: "logic replaces wire everywhere", or says `reg` infers a flip-flop.
questions.model_answer:
`logic` is a 4-state data type; `reg` is the same type under an older, misleading name (it does not imply a register; §6.11.2). `wire` is a net. The difference that matters is the kind of object:

- A variable (declared with `logic`) may be written by any number of procedural statements (last write wins), or by exactly one continuous assignment or one port, never a mix (§6.5).

- A net may have many drivers; its value comes from the net type's resolution function. Nets cannot be assigned procedurally.

So: (1) is an error, two continuous assignments to a variable. (2) is legal: two drivers on a net, resolved (one drives `z`, so the other wins; if both drove different values the result would be `x`). (3) is an error: `y_var` is written by `always_comb` and by a continuous assignment; `always_comb` also forbids writes from any other process (§9.2.2.2).

Ports. In an ANSI port list, an `input logic` port is a net by default, while an `output logic` port is a variable (§23.2.2.3). So you can drive an output from `always_ff`, but you cannot procedurally assign an input inside the module.

Use a net when a signal has more than one driver: tri-state buses, `inout` pads, wired logic, or several modules driving one signal by design. Use `logic` for everything with a single driver; the compiler then catches accidental second drivers for you.
follow_ups: Why does the `default_nettype none` compiler directive help catch bugs, and what does it change?
What does a net with two drivers of `1` and `0` resolve to? Of `1` and `z`?
Can you write `input var logic a` and what changes?
common_mistakes: Believing a `logic` variable resolves multiple `assign` drivers like a wire.
Believing `reg` means the signal becomes a flop.
Assuming `input logic` is a variable that can be assigned inside the module.

questions.prompt: Write a `typedef` enum for a 2-bit opcode (`RD`, `WR`, `IDLE`) and a packed struct for a 16-bit command header: opcode, 6-bit length, 8-bit address. Then predict what the code below prints, and explain the difference between the static cast and `$cast`.
questions.rubric: Strong: correct enum and packed struct with the MSB-first rule; predicts the empty name and the failed `$cast`; explains static cast (no check) versus `$cast` (checked, returns 0 as a function); knows the enum's default initial value comes from its base type. Weak: says the static cast errors at run time, or that a packed struct's first member is the least significant.
questions.model_answer:
```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [1:0] {RD, WR, IDLE} op_e;     // RD=0, WR=1, IDLE=2

typedef struct packed {
  op_e        op;      // bits [15:14]: first member is most significant
  logic [5:0] len;     // bits [13:8]
  logic [7:0] addr;    // bits [7:0]
} cmd_hdr_t;

cmd_hdr_t   hdr;
logic [15:0] bus;
assign bus = hdr;      // a packed struct is one 16-bit vector
```

A packed struct has no gaps and its first member is the most significant (§7.2.1). Used as a whole it is a single vector, so it can be assigned to a bus, compared, or streamed. An unpacked struct has implementation-dependent layout and cannot be used as a vector.

Prediction.

1. The static cast `op_e'(raw)` (§6.24.1) converts the value to the enum's base type without checking that it is a member (§6.19.4); §6.24.2 calls it a coercion that always succeeds at run time. `op` now holds 3, which is not a member, so `op.name()` returns an empty string (§6.19.5.6). It prints `[] 3`.

2. `$cast` called as a function checks that 3 is a legal `op_e` value. It is not, so `$cast` returns 0, leaves `op` unchanged and the message prints (§6.24.2).

Rule: use `$cast` (or a range check) whenever the value comes from outside your code: a DUT bus, a file, a plusarg. Use the static cast only when you have already proved the value is legal.

Also note: a variable of this enum starts as `'x`, the default of its `logic` base type, not as `RD` (§6.8, Table 6-7). With an `int` base type it would start at 0, which happens to equal the first member and hides a missing reset.
follow_ups: What happens if you call `$cast(op, raw)` as a task instead of a function and the value is illegal?
When would you use a packed union, and what must be true of its members?
How would you print every member of `op_e` without hard-coding the names?
common_mistakes: Using a static cast on DUT data and never noticing illegal opcodes.
Assuming the first struct member occupies the low bits.
Assuming an enum variable starts at its first member.

questions.prompt: Predict the result (0, 1 or x) of each expression, with `a = 4'b10x1`. Which operator would you use in a checker that must flag any unknown bit?
questions.rubric: Strong: x, 1, x, 1, 1, x with reasons; knows `==?` wildcards only the right operand and `inside` uses `==?` with the set on the right; uses `$isunknown` for X detection and `===` for intentional X/Z expectations. Weak: treats `==?` as symmetric, says (1) or (3) is 0 (no known bit differs, so both are x), or uses `===` against known values as an X check.
questions.model_answer:
1. x. No known bit differs, and bit 1 is `x` on both sides, so the relation is ambiguous (§11.4.5); a known differing bit would give a definite 0.

2. 1. Case equality compares `x` and `z` literally and never returns `x` (§11.4.5).

3. x. Every known bit matches and bit 1 is `x` versus `0`, so the relation is ambiguous and the result is unknown. In an `if`, unknown counts as false (§12.4).

4. 1. Wildcard equality treats `x`, `z` (and `?`) in the right operand as don't-care (§11.4.6). Bit 1 of the right side is `?`, so the `x` in `a` is ignored.

5. 1. Here `a` is the right operand, so its `x` in bit 1 acts as a wildcard. The other bits (1, 0, 1) match, so the result is 1.

6. x. `inside` uses `==?` for integral values, with each set member as the right operand (§11.4.13). Neither member has a wildcard, the `x` in `a` is not a wildcard on the left, so both comparisons are `x`. With no match and some `x` results, `inside` returns `x`.

Lines 4 and 5 are the classic trap: only the right operand of `==?` can carry wildcards, so swapping the operands changes what counts as a don't-care.

For a checker: do not rely on `==` to catch X: it yields `x` (or a definite 0 if a known bit differs), `if` takes the `else` branch, and the message is misleading. Test for unknowns explicitly with `$isunknown(sig)` (§20.9), then compare with `==`. Use `===` when the *expected* value deliberately contains `x` or `z`, for example checking that a bus is tri-stated (`bus === 'z`).
follow_ups: What does `!(a == 4'b1001)` evaluate to, and what does an `if` do with it?
Why are `===` and `!==` illegal inside constraints?
How do `casez` and `casex` treat `z` and `x` in the case expression and the items?
common_mistakes: Assuming `==?` treats wildcards on both sides.
Assuming `==` always returns x when an operand holds X; a known bit that differs still gives 0.
Using `inside` on 4-state DUT values and expecting unknown bits to fail the test.

questions.prompt: The DUT's `status` output is `8'bxxxx_0000` because a register was never reset. Predict what the checker below reports in each case, and explain how X can be hidden both by 2-state types and by 4-state code.
questions.rubric: Strong: predicts A, B-else, C-idle, D correctly with clauses; names both hiding mechanisms (2-state conversion and X in conditions); gives explicit unknown checks and `===` with the right use. Weak: only says "X becomes 0 in 2-state" and misses that 4-state `if` also hides X, or thinks `==` with X raises an error.
questions.model_answer:
- A prints: a 4-state value converted to a 2-state type turns every `x` and `z` bit into 0 (§6.11.2), so `st2 == 8'h00` is true. The reset bug is gone from the testbench's view.

- B prints "not equal": the low four bits match and the upper four are `x` against 0, so the relation is ambiguous and the result is `x` (§11.4.5), and an `if` whose condition is `x` takes the else branch (§12.4). The checker reports the wrong reason and does not mention X at all.

- C prints "idle": same rule; `status[7]` is `x`, so the `if` is false. This is X-optimism: 4-state code that silently picks a branch.

- D prints: `$isunknown` returns 1 if any bit is `x` or `z` (§20.9).

So X is hidden two ways: by copying into 2-state types, and by `if`/`case` treating an unknown condition as false. Defences:

1. Keep DUT-facing data `logic` all the way into the checker.

2. Check for unknowns explicitly before comparing: `if ($isunknown(status)) $error(...)`, or an assertion such as `assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !$isunknown(status));`.

3. Use `===`/`!==` when the expected value itself may contain `x` or `z`; it compares those bits exactly and never returns `x` (§11.4.5).

4. In RTL review, look for `if`/`case` on signals that can be unknown after reset.
follow_ups: What does `status === 8'bxxxx_0000` return, and when is that comparison useful?
How does a `case` statement treat an `x` selector compared with `casez` and `casex`?
Why might gate-level simulation show X where RTL showed a clean value (X-pessimism vs X-optimism)?
common_mistakes: Thinking `==` with an X operand raises an error or can be true; it gives x when the known bits agree (as here) or a definite 0 when a known bit differs, and `if` treats both as false.
Converting DUT outputs to `int` or `bit` in monitors "for speed".
Using `===` against a fully known expected value and believing it checks for X; it just compares.

questions.prompt: Predict the value of each result and the output of the `if`. Explain the sizing and signedness rules that decide each one.
questions.rubric: Strong: 5'h10, 4'h0, 5'h00, "not less", each tied to context- vs self-determined sizing and the any-unsigned rule; mentions part-selects and concatenations are unsigned. Weak: gets (3) wrong because it ignores self-determined concatenation operands, or claims an `int` comparison is always signed.
questions.model_answer:
1. 5'h10. Operands of `+` are context-determined: the expression is evaluated at the width of the largest operand *including the left-hand side*, here 5 bits, so the carry is kept (§11.6.1, §11.6.2).

2. 4'h0. Same rule with a 4-bit target: the carry is lost.

3. 5'h00. Operands of a concatenation are self-determined (§11.6.1, Table 11-21). `a + b` is evaluated at 4 bits, giving 0, and the 4-bit concatenation is then zero-extended to 5 bits.

4. "not less". If any operand is unsigned, the comparison is unsigned (§11.8.1). `u` is unsigned, so `i` is treated as unsigned: both are extended to 32 bits and `-1` becomes `32'hFFFF_FFFF`, which is not less than 1.

The rules in one place:

- Width: find the largest operand in the context-determined part of the expression, including the assignment target; evaluate everything at that width (§11.8.2).

- Some operands are always self-determined: concatenation members, shift amounts, the condition of `?:`, and the operands of `&&`, `||`, `!` and the reduction operators (Table 11-21).

- Relational and equality operands are sized to the larger of the two, independent of the surrounding expression, and the result is a 1-bit unsigned value (Table 11-21, §11.8.1).

- Sign: decimal literals are signed, based literals (`8'd1`) unsigned unless written with `s`; part-selects, bit-selects and concatenations are always unsigned (§11.8.1). One unsigned operand makes the whole context unsigned.

Fixes: widen explicitly (`s5 = 5'(a) + b;`) and make intent explicit with `$signed(u)` or by declaring `u` as `logic signed [7:0]`. Many lint tools warn on mixed-sign comparisons; turn that warning on.
follow_ups: What does `logic signed [7:0] x = -8'sd1; logic [15:0] y = x[7:0];` store in `y`, and why?
Why does `(a + b) >> 1` lose the carry for 16-bit `a` and `b`, and how do you fix it?
What width is the result of `a * b` for two 8-bit operands assigned to a 32-bit variable?
common_mistakes: Believing an expression's width is just its widest operand, ignoring the assignment target.
Believing one signed operand makes a comparison signed.
Forgetting that a part-select of a signed variable is unsigned.

questions.prompt: Explain packed versus unpacked arrays using the two declarations below. What do `w`, `w[3]`, `w[3:2]` and `b[1:2]` select? How do you turn `b` into one 32-bit word, and what byte-order bug is common when you do?
questions.code:
```systemverilog
logic [3:0][7:0] w;       // packed: 4 bytes
logic [7:0]      b [4];   // unpacked: 4 separate bytes, b[0]..b[3]
logic [31:0]     word;
```
questions.rubric: Strong: `w` as one vector; `w[3]` byte, `w[3:2]` two bytes; recognises `w[31:0]` as a wrong select; states unpacked arrays can be sliced (`b[1:2]`) but not used as a vector; correct `{>>{b}}` mapping and the `{<<8{b}}` reversal; names a byte-order bug. Weak: "unpacked arrays cannot be sliced", or `w[31:0]` as the whole word, or a C-style "reads adjacent memory" explanation.
questions.model_answer:
A packed array is one contiguous vector subdivided into fields. Used as a whole, `w` is a single 32-bit value (§7.4.1). Selects work along the leftmost packed dimension first:

- `w[3]` is the most significant byte (8 bits).

- `w[3:2]` is the top two bytes (16 bits), as in the LRM's `joe[7][3:2]` example (§7.4.4, §7.4.5).

- `w[3][7]` is a single bit.

- `w[31:0]` is not the flat word: it is a range of elements 31..0 of the 4-element byte dimension. Tools may reject it at compile time; otherwise elements beyond 3 read `x` (§11.5.1). The flat word is just `w`: a packed array used as a primary is one vector (§7.4.1). If you want an explicit cast, use a size cast, `32'(w)`, or a type name: `typedef logic [31:0] word_t;` and then `word_t'(w)`. `logic [31:0]'(w)` is not legal: a casting type must be a built-in type keyword without dimensions, a type or parameter name, a constant size, `signed`/`unsigned`, `string` or `const` (§6.24.1, Syntax 6-7).

An unpacked array is a collection of separate elements. Unpacked arrays can be indexed and sliced one dimension at a time: `b[1:2]` is an unpacked array of two bytes, assignable to another two-element array (§7.4.5). What you cannot do is treat `b` as a bit vector: assigning it directly to `word` is a compile error. Convert with streaming or a bit-stream cast (§11.4.14, §6.24.3):

```systemverilog
word = {>>{b}};     // b[0] lands in word[31:24], b[3] in word[7:0]
word = {<<8{b}};    // byte order reversed: b[0] lands in word[7:0]
```

The common bug is choosing the wrong stream direction (or declaring `[0:3][7:0]` instead of `[3:0][7:0]`). The data is all there, so nothing fails until a checker compares against a little-endian reference model and every multi-byte field is byte-swapped.

Use packed for buses and fields you want to treat as numbers. Use unpacked for memories, register files and anything indexed element by element. An out-of-range read on an unpacked array returns the element type's default value rather than another element's data (§7.4.5, Table 7-1).
follow_ups: What does `{<<{b}}` (no slice size) produce compared with `{<<8{b}}`?
Can you assign a 32-bit packed vector to `logic [7:0] b[4]` with a cast? Which syntax?
Why does a packed struct often replace a packed array for protocol headers?
common_mistakes: Writing `w[31:0]` to mean the whole packed array.
Saying unpacked arrays cannot be sliced; they can, one dimension at a time.
Picking `<<` or `>>` by trial and error instead of from the element-order rule.

questions.prompt: Predict the output of each line. What type does each method return, and what goes wrong with the checksum and the sort?
questions.rubric: Strong: predicts 54 and 310 and explains the element-type rule (§7.12.3); knows locator methods return queues; sort is in place and void; needs a `with` key for handles. Weak: predicts 310 for (1), or uses `sum()` on bytes for checksums without widening.
questions.model_answer:
1. 54. A reduction method returns the element type unless a `with` clause gives another type (§7.12.3). 200 + 100 + 10 = 310, which wraps in 8 bits to 310 - 256 = 54.

2. 310. The `with (int'(item))` clause makes the reduction work on `int`, so nothing wraps. Always widen when you compute checksums or byte counts.

3. '{1, 3}. Locator methods return a queue: `find_index` returns the indices of every match (§7.12.1).

4. '{1, 1, 4, 5}. `sort()` reorders the array in place, ascending, and returns nothing (§7.12.2). (The exact text that `%p` prints varies by tool.)

Sorting objects. For a queue of class handles, `sort()` needs a key: `q.sort() with (item.addr);`. The `with` expression must have relational operators defined; class handles do not, so a bare `sort()` on handles is an error (§7.12.2).

Practical uses: `find_index`/`find` to pull matching items out of an expected list; `sum() with` for checksums and byte counts; `sort() with (item.addr)` to normalise two lists before an order-independent compare; `unique()` to find distinct IDs.
follow_ups: What does `q.find_first with (item > 10)` return if nothing matches?
What is `item.index` and when would you use it inside a `with` clause?
How does `unique()` differ from `unique_index()`?
common_mistakes: Expecting `sum()` to return a wide integer.
Expecting `find_index` to return a single `int`.
Calling `sort()` without a key on a queue of class handles.

questions.prompt: Compare dynamic arrays, queues and associative arrays. For each, give a testbench use, and explain why a bounded queue is not a model of a hardware FIFO.
questions.code:
```systemverilog
byte        payload[];          // dynamic array
int         q[$];               // queue
int         q4[$:3];            // bounded queue: at most 4 elements
my_txn      exp_by_id[int];     // associative array keyed by ID

initial begin
  payload = new[8];
  payload = new[16](payload);   // resize and keep the first 8
  repeat (6) q4.push_back(1);   // what is q4.size()?
end
```
questions.rubric: Strong: correct structure, cost and a realistic TB use for each (payload sized at run time, in-order list, sparse or by-ID map); `new[N]` vs `new[N](old)`; missing-key behaviour; the bounded-queue discard rule with the size prediction and the mailbox alternative. Weak: "bounded queues model FIFO depth" without the discard caveat, or a use such as "coverage bins" for dynamic arrays.
questions.model_answer:
- Dynamic array (§7.5): contiguous, sized at run time with `new[N]`, constant-time indexing. `new[N]` alone discards the old contents; `new[N](old)` copies them. Use it for a packet payload whose length is chosen when the packet is randomized.

- Queue (§7.10): ordered, grows and shrinks at both ends in constant time (`push_back`, `pop_front`), with constant-time indexing. Use it for an in-order expected list in a scoreboard or a driver's pending list.

- Associative array (§7.8, §7.9): sparse, keyed by any index type, traversed in index order with `first`/`next`. Use it for a sparse memory model or an expected-by-ID table for out-of-order completions. Reading a missing key returns the type's default value and issues a warning (§7.8.6), so check `exists()` first.

Bounded queues. `q4[$:3]` may hold at most 4 elements. After any write that leaves elements beyond the bound, those elements are discarded and a warning is issued (§7.10.5). So the 5th and 6th `push_back` drop the new values and `q4.size()` is 4. A hardware FIFO blocks the writer or raises a `full` flag; a bounded queue does neither, it just loses data with a warning. To model back-pressure, check `size()` against the depth explicitly, or use a bounded mailbox, whose `put()` suspends the caller until there is room (§15.4.1, §15.4.3).

Memory hygiene. Delete entries from queues and associative arrays when they are matched, and report what is left at the end of the test.
follow_ups: What does `q.insert(1, x)` cost? Is that guaranteed by the LRM?
Which index types can an associative array use, and how does iteration order depend on them?
How would you model a FIFO with depth 4 that back-pressures a driver?
common_mistakes: Assuming `new[N]` keeps the old elements.
Expecting a bounded queue to block or error on overflow; it discards with a warning (§7.10.5).
Reading `exp_by_id[id]` without `exists()` and comparing against a default-constructed (null) handle.

questions.prompt: An out-of-order scoreboard keeps expected transactions in one queue and searches it with `find_first_index` for every observed transaction. Simulation slows as traffic grows. What does the LRM guarantee about queue operation costs, and how would you restructure the scoreboard?
questions.rubric: Strong: states what §7.10 guarantees and labels middle-insert cost as implementation behaviour; identifies the linear search as the actual cost; proposes keyed storage (associative array of queues) that keeps per-ID order and deletes empty keys. Weak: states "insert is O(N)" as a language fact and proposes nothing about the search.
follow_ups: How do you handle a protocol where order is guaranteed only per ID and per direction?
What end-of-test check do you add, and in which UVM phase?
When would sorting the expected queue be acceptable?
common_mistakes: Quoting big-O costs for queue operations as if the LRM defined them.
Optimizing insertion while leaving a linear search on every observed transaction.

questions.prompt: Long regressions slow down and eventually run out of memory. The scoreboard below is the prime suspect. Find the leak and any latent risk, fix them, and add the end-of-test checks that would have caught the problem early.
questions.rubric: Strong: finds the missing delete; names the unbounded analysis FIFO as a latent risk (drained here, but unbounded if the draining thread stops) and checks `used()` at the end; fixes delete on both match and mismatch; handles unexpected and duplicate tags; adds a `check_phase` leftover check (pending and FIFO). Weak: only "call delete" with no end-of-test check, claims the FIFO itself grows in this code, or puts a blocking wait in `write`.
questions.model_answer:
The leak: entries are never deleted. `write_actual` compares but never calls `pending.delete(a.tag)`, so every expected transaction stays in the associative array for the whole run (§7.8, §7.9). Memory grows with traffic, and expectations for traffic that never happens pile up here too.

A latent risk, not a leak in this code: the analysis FIFO is unbounded. `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` is constructed with an unbounded size so that `write` can never block (uvm-core 2020.3.1 `uvm_tlm_fifos.svh`: "analysis fifo must be unbounded"). Here `run_phase` drains `exp_fifo` into `pending` forever, so the FIFO stays nearly empty. But if that draining thread ever blocks, stalls or is killed, the FIFO grows without limit and nothing warns you. The `used()` check at the end of the test catches it.

Fixes:

```systemverilog
function void write_actual(my_txn a);
  if (!pending.exists(a.tag)) begin
    `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("unexpected tag %0d", a.tag))
    return;
  end
  if (!pending[a.tag].compare(a))
    `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("mismatch tag %0d", a.tag))
  pending.delete(a.tag);                  // free the entry either way
endfunction

function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  if (pending.num() != 0)
    `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("%0d expected transactions never seen", pending.num()))
  if (exp_fifo.used() != 0)
    `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("%0d expectations left in exp_fifo", exp_fifo.used()))
endfunction
```

Put the leftover check in `check_phase` (IEEE 1800.2-2020 9.8.1.7), which exists for exactly this, rather than `report_phase`. Also watch for a reused tag overwriting an entry that was never matched: `pending[e.tag] = e` silently replaces it, so check `exists()` first and flag duplicates. In very long tests, also report the high-water mark of `pending.num()` periodically; a steady climb is the early warning.
follow_ups: How would you detect expectations that will never complete because the DUT dropped them, before the end of the test?
Why can `write()` on an analysis port never block, and what does that imply for subscriber design?
How would you measure memory growth per component in a regression?
common_mistakes: Deleting only on a successful compare, so mismatching entries leak.
Assuming every TLM FIFO is bounded; `uvm_tlm_fifo` defaults to size 1, but the analysis FIFO is unbounded.
Overwriting a pending entry when a tag is reused and losing the original silently.

questions.prompt: Explain blocking (`=`) and nonblocking (`<=`) assignments. Both versions below start with `q1 = q2 = q3 = 0` and `d = 1`. Predict `q1`, `q2` and `q3` after the first rising edge of `clk`, and say which version is a 3-stage shift register.
questions.rubric: Strong: defines both by *when the update happens* (immediately, or scheduled for the NBA region), predicts 1/0/0 and 1/1/1, names A as the shift register, and explains the inter-process race (§4.7) as the reason flops use `<=`. Gives the `always_ff`/`always_comb` rule. Senior signal: the program/checker nuance (Reactive and Re-NBA). Weak: "blocking runs in order, nonblocking runs in parallel" with no update timing, or claims an NBA updates at a later simulation time.
questions.model_answer:
A blocking assignment `=` evaluates its right-hand side and updates the variable before the next statement runs. A nonblocking assignment `<=` evaluates its right-hand side when the statement executes but only *schedules* the update. In module code the update matures in the NBA region, after every process woken by the edge has already read the old values (§10.4.1, §10.4.2, §4.4.2.4).

Version A gives `q1 = 1, q2 = 0, q3 = 0`. Each right-hand side reads the value from before the edge, so `d` moves one stage per clock: this is the 3-stage shift register.

Version B gives `q1 = 1, q2 = 1, q3 = 1`. Each statement sees the value the previous statement has just written, so `d` falls through all three in one edge. Synthesis builds one flop driving three outputs, and reordering the three lines changes the hardware.

Why flops use `<=`. Two `always` blocks triggered by the same edge may run in either order (§4.7). If one writes `a = b` and the other `b = a`, the result depends on that order: a race. With `<=` every process reads before any variable updates, so the order no longer matters.

Rules of thumb: `<=` in `always_ff`; `=` in `always_comb`, where later statements must see earlier results; never assign one variable with both (a style rule, not an LRM rule). Expert nuance: the Active/NBA description is for module code. Blocking assignments in program blocks and checkers run in the Reactive region, and their nonblocking updates mature in Re-NBA (§4.4.2.6, §4.4.2.8).
follow_ups: What do `a <= b; b <= a;` and `a = b; b = a;` each do at one edge?
A `$display(q1)` placed right after `q1 <= d;` prints which value? What would `$strobe` print?
Is `x <= 1;` legal if `x` is an automatic variable or an element of a queue? (No: §10.4.2 forbids NBAs to automatic variables and to elements of dynamically sized arrays.)
common_mistakes: Saying a nonblocking assignment updates "in the next cycle" or at a later simulation time. It updates in the same time step, in the NBA region.
Believing `<=` everywhere removes all races. A testbench that drives with `=` at the active edge still races the DUT.
Using `<=` inside `always_comb` for multi-statement logic, so later statements read stale values within the same pass.

questions.prompt: When do you use `always_comb`, `always @*`, `always_latch` and `always_ff`? Give at least three concrete ways `always_comb` behaves differently from `always @*`.
questions.code:
```systemverilog
function automatic logic parity(input logic [7:0] d);
  return ^(d ^ mask);           // reads module variable `mask`
endfunction

always_comb  y1 = parity(data); // (A)
always @*    y2 = parity(data); // (B)
```
questions.rubric: Strong: right procedure for each style; at least three LRM differences (time-zero evaluation, function-body sensitivity, single-writer rule, no blocking statements) with the `mask` example explained; mentions latch warnings. Weak: "always_comb is just shorthand for always @*".
questions.model_answer:
- `always_ff`: sequential logic. One event control, no blocking timing controls inside, written with `<=` (§9.2.2.4).

- `always_comb`: combinational logic. Inferred sensitivity, written with `=` (§9.2.2.2).

- `always_latch`: intended latches. Same rules as `always_comb`, but tools check that it really is latched logic (§9.2.2.3).

- `always @*`: the older general-purpose form. It still works, but gives fewer guarantees.

How `always_comb` differs from `always @*` (§9.2.2.2.2):

1. Runs once at time zero, after all `initial` and `always` procedures have started, so outputs are consistent with inputs from the start. `always @*` waits for its first input change; if inputs never change, its output stays at its initial value (`x` for `logic`).

2. Sees inside called functions. In the code above, (A) is sensitive to `mask` because `parity` reads it. (B) is sensitive only to `data`, the argument, so a change of `mask` alone does not update `y2`: a simulation-only bug that synthesis will not reproduce.

3. Single writer. Variables written by `always_comb` (including in functions it calls) cannot be written by any other process; `always @*` allows it.

4. No blocking. `always_comb` may not contain timing or event controls or `fork`.

5. Expressions in immediate assertions inside called functions also join the sensitivity list.

Tools should warn when an `always_comb` infers a latch, for example an `if` without an `else` (§9.2.2.2). That warning is one of the main reasons to prefer the specialized forms: they state intent, and the tool checks it.
follow_ups: An `always_comb` block calls a task. What does the task body contribute to the sensitivity list?
What does `always_ff @(posedge clk iff en)` do?
Why can a missing `default` in a `case` inside `always_comb` create a latch?
common_mistakes: Treating `always_comb` and `always @*` as identical.
Writing a variable from both `always_comb` and another process.
Putting `#` delays or `@` inside `always_comb`.

questions.prompt: For `sel` values 0 through 7, which of these three statements report a violation, and which branch runs? Are `unique` and `priority` only synthesis hints?
questions.rubric: Strong: correct violation sets (unique: 3,5,6,7; priority: 4–7; unique0: none), first-match for priority, overlap rule for unique; explains run-time semantics, deferral to Observed with glitch flushing, and the synthesis mismatch risk. Weak: "unique is a synthesis pragma", or expects unique0 to report missing values.
questions.model_answer:
- `unique case`: reports a violation for 3, 5, 6 and 7, because no item matches, and it would also report if two items matched the same value (§12.5.3). For 0–2 and 4 exactly one item matches and that branch runs. With no match, no branch runs, so `y` keeps its old value.

- `priority casez`: acts on the first match only. Values 0 and 1 match both items; that is allowed, and `A` runs. 2 and 3 run `B`. Values 4–7 match nothing, so it reports a violation (§12.5.3).

- `unique0 case`: like `unique` for overlaps, but no violation when nothing matches (§12.5.3). 3, 5, 6, 7 silently do nothing.

They are not only synthesis hints. They are run-time checks with defined simulation semantics: the simulator must issue the violation report. The report is deferred to the Observed region and is flushed if the process re-runs in the same time step, so zero-delay glitches in combinational logic do not produce false reports (§12.4.2.1). Violation reports can be controlled with the assertion control tasks (§20.11).

Why it matters. Synthesis may build parallel (unique) or priority logic and treat unlisted values as don't-care. If simulation silently ignored unlisted values, you would sign off an RTL behaviour that the gates do not have. The violation report is the simulator telling you that your assumption was wrong.
follow_ups: What is the difference between `unique case` with a `default` and `unique0 case`?
Why is a deferred violation report flushed when an `always_comb` re-triggers in the same time step?
How would you turn these reports off during reset without editing the RTL?
common_mistakes: Treating `unique`/`priority` as comments for synthesis.
Expecting `priority` to flag overlapping items.
Adding a `default` to a `unique case` and losing the violation check for unlisted values.

questions.prompt: Explain `fork...join`, `join_any` and `join_none`. Then read the task below: which value of `i` does each `send_pkt` call receive, and which threads does the final `disable fork` kill? Rewrite it so that only the timeout race is cleaned up.
questions.code:
```systemverilog
task automatic run_body();
  fork
    monitor_bus();                 // meant to run for the whole test
  join_none

  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
    fork
      send_pkt(i);
    join_none
  end

  fork
    wait_for_irq();
    #1us $display("timeout");
  join_any
  disable fork;
endtask
```
questions.rubric: Strong: correct semantics of all three, including that join_any leaves siblings running and that join_none children start when the parent blocks; predicts 3/3/3 with the reason; states disable fork kills all descendants (§9.6.3) and names the monitor as collateral; gives the isolation wrapper and the `automatic` copy. Weak: says join_any kills the other branches, that join_none children start immediately, or that disable fork only affects the most recent fork.
questions.model_answer:
- `join` waits for all children.

- `join_any` waits for the first child to finish; the others keep running.

- `join_none` does not wait. The children are scheduled, but they start only when the parent blocks or finishes (§9.3.2).

Loop capture. The three `join_none` forks do not start until the parent blocks at the third `fork`. By then the loop has finished and `i == 3`, so every `send_pkt` sees 3. The LRM example in §9.3.2 shows the same effect. Fix it by copying the value in the fork's declaration area, which is initialized when the fork is entered, before the process is spawned:

```systemverilog
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
  fork
    automatic int k = i;
    send_pkt(k);
  join_none
end
```

`disable fork` kills every descendant of the calling process, not just the last fork's children (§9.6.3). Here it kills `monitor_bus`, any `send_pkt` still running, and the losing branch of the race. Isolate the race in its own process so `disable fork` only sees that process's children:

```systemverilog
fork begin
  fork
    wait_for_irq();
    #1us $display("timeout");
  join_any
  disable fork;          // kills only the race's leftovers
end join
```

Use `wait fork` to wait for all children of the current process (§9.6.1). For finer control, keep `process` handles and `kill()` a specific thread (§9.7).
follow_ups: What does `wait fork` wait for, and why can it hang a test that has forked a forever-running monitor?
How would you kill only `send_pkt` number 1 without touching the others?
Why is `disable <block_name>` riskier than `disable fork` in reusable code?
common_mistakes: Expecting each `join_none` child to see its own loop value without an `automatic` copy.
Calling `disable fork` after `join_any` in a task that forked long-lived threads earlier.
Assuming `join_any` stops the other children.

questions.prompt: Two initial blocks call `send` at the same time with different addresses. What goes wrong, and how do you fix it? While you are there, explain `ref` and `const ref` arguments and when you would use them.
questions.rubric: Strong: identifies static-by-default storage shared across concurrent calls (§13.3.1); fixes with `automatic`; notes class methods are automatic; explains input/output copy timing, `ref` aliasing and `const ref`; mentions the explicit-`static` initializer rule. Weak: blames the clock edge or a race, or says module tasks are automatic by default.
questions.model_answer:
Tasks and functions declared in a module, interface, program or package are static by default: one copy of every argument and local variable is shared by all concurrent calls (§13.3.1, §13.3.2). The second call overwrites `addr`, `len` and `i` while the first is waiting at `@(posedge clk)`, so both threads drive addresses from whichever call wrote last, and the loop counter is shared.

Fix: make the task automatic, so every call gets its own copy on the stack:

```systemverilog
task automatic send(input int addr, input int len);
  for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) begin
    @(posedge clk);
    bus_addr <= addr + i;
  end
endtask
```

Methods in classes are always automatic (§13.3.1), which is one reason class-based testbenches rarely hit this bug. A related trap: a variable with an initializer inside a static task or block must be declared `static` explicitly, because the initializer runs only once at the start of simulation, not on each call (§6.21).

Argument passing (§13.5):

- `input` copies the value in at the call; `output` copies out at the end.

- `ref` passes a reference: no copy, and the callee sees changes the caller makes while the task is running (and vice versa). Use it for large arrays or for a task that must watch a caller's variable over time. `ref` arguments require automatic subroutines.

- `const ref` passes a reference the callee cannot modify: the efficient way to pass a large array or queue read-only (§13.5.2).
follow_ups: Why must a task with a `ref` argument be automatic?

In a `fork...join_none` inside a task, why is referring to a `ref` argument restricted? (The actual may be an automatic variable that is gone by the time the forked process runs, so §9.3.2 forbids it except in the fork's variable initializers. A `ref static` argument, new in IEEE 1800-2023, accepts only actuals with static lifetime and lifts the restriction, §13.5.2.)
When would you deliberately declare one variable `static` inside an automatic task?
common_mistakes: Assuming module tasks are automatic like class methods.
Passing a large queue by value to a function called millions of times.
Writing `int count = 0;` inside a static task and expecting it to reset on every call.

questions.prompt: Which of the four functions below compile? For each one that does not, name the rule it breaks. Then, with the illegal ones removed, predict what the simulation prints, and say when you would write a task rather than a function.
questions.rubric: Strong: rejects (1) for the time control and (2) for enabling a task, whether or not the task waits; accepts (3) and explains the exception for work that does not block, including `fork...join_none`, whose process waits after the function returns; spots the implicit 1-bit return type of (4) and predicts `0: f3 returned, f4 = 1` then `5: edge after f3`; picks a task when the code must consume time and a function when it must return a value in zero time. Weak: says a function may call a task that never waits, says a function can never contain `fork`, or predicts `f4 = 5`.
questions.model_answer:
The rule behind all four: a function must return without suspending the process that called it, because a call to it can sit inside an expression (§13.2, §13.4).

1. Does not compile. `@(posedge clk)` is a time-controlling statement. A function shall not contain `#`, `##`, `@`, `fork...join`, `fork...join_any`, `wait`, `wait fork`, `wait_order` or `expect` (§13.4, rule a).

2. Does not compile. A function shall not enable a task, whether or not that task contains time controls (§13.4, rule b). Make `f2` a task, or move the call to the caller.

3. Compiles. Statements that do not block are allowed in a function: nonblocking assignments, event triggers, clocking drives and `fork...join_none` (§13.4.4). The forked process may contain anything a task may contain, but it runs on its own after `f3` has returned, so `f3` still takes zero time.

4. Compiles, with a trap. No return type was written, so the return type is a scalar `logic` (§13.4). `return a + b` keeps only bit 0 of 5, so `f4(2, 3)` is 1. Always write the return type, or `void`.

With (1) and (2) removed, the simulation prints:

```text
0: f3 returned, f4 = 1
5: edge after f3
```

`f3` returns at time 0. The process it forked waits for the first rising edge of `clk`: `clk` starts at 0 and first rises at 5.

Choosing between them:

- Write a task when the code must consume time: drive a protocol, wait for a handshake or a clock. A task can call tasks and functions, and returns results through `output` or `ref` arguments.

- Write a function when the code must finish in zero time: an expected value, a CRC, a parity bit, a formatted message. A nonvoid function can be an operand in an expression; a `void` function is called as a statement (§13.4.1). The compiler then guarantees the code cannot block.

- Functions can take the same argument directions as tasks, including `output` and `ref` (§13.4), and may kill, suspend or resume another process (§13.4, rule c).

- Calling a nonvoid function as a statement is legal but gives a warning; `void'(f())` discards the result on purpose (§13.4.1).

UVM uses the same split: `build_phase` and `connect_phase` are functions and `run_phase` is a task (uvm-core 2020.3.1 `uvm_component.svh`), so nothing can wait while the testbench is being built.
follow_ups: Why is `bit y = check();` illegal when `check` is a function containing `fork...join_none`, while calling it from an `initial` block is legal? (§13.4.4: such a function must be called from a thread created by an `initial` or `always` procedure, or by a fork in one, not from a variable initializer.)
You need a zero-time helper that returns two values. Task or function, and how does it return them?
What does `void'(q.pop_front())` do, and why is the cast there?
common_mistakes: Believing a function may call a task as long as the task never waits.
Believing a function can never contain `fork`; `fork...join_none` is allowed (§13.4.4).
Leaving out the return type and getting a 1-bit result.
sources: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_component.svh (build_phase and connect_phase are functions, run_phase is a task)

questions.prompt: `q` is 0 before the edge and `d` is 1. Predict every line printed at the rising edge of `clk`, and explain when `$display`, `$strobe` and `$monitor` each print.
questions.rubric: Strong: D shows 0, S and M show 1, with the NBA/Postponed reasoning; knows `$monitor` excludes `$time` from its trigger list and that only one monitor is active. Weak: says `$display` shows 1 because it runs "after the clock", or that `$strobe` runs in the NBA region.
questions.model_answer:
`$monitor` sets up a watch on its arguments. From then on it prints at the end of any time step in which one of them changed; a change of `$time` alone does not count (§21.2.3).

At the edge:

- `D: q=0`. `$display` prints immediately when the statement executes. The `initial` block resumes in the Active region, before the nonblocking update of `q` matures in the NBA region, so it sees the old value. (Strictly, the initial block and `always_ff` may run in either order, but the NBA update is always later, so the result is the same.)

- `S: q=1`. `$strobe` prints at the end of the time step, after all updates, in the Postponed region (§21.2.2, §4.4.2.9).

- `M: t=<edge time> q=1`. `q` changed in this time step, so `$monitor` prints at the end of the step, also from the Postponed region.

Rules worth knowing: only one `$monitor` list is active at a time, and a new `$monitor` call replaces the previous one; `$monitoroff`/`$monitoron` pause and resume it (§21.2.3). Use `$display` for event-driven messages, `$strobe` when you need settled end-of-step values, and avoid `$monitor` in large testbenches because it prints on every change.
follow_ups: Would `$display` after `#0` show the new value? Why is that a fragile habit?
What prints if you call `$monitor` twice with different arguments?
What is the difference between `$write` and `$display`?
common_mistakes: Expecting `$display` at the clock edge to show the post-edge value of a flop.
Using several `$monitor` calls and expecting all of them to stay active.

questions.prompt: With the `timescale 1ns/100ps` directive, predict what `$time` and `$realtime` print in the code below, and when `set` actually changes. Why can two modules with different time units disagree about "the same" delay?
questions.rubric: Strong: rounding of delays to precision (1.6, 3.2 ns); `$time` rounded to the unit (2, 3); `$realtime` 1.60/3.20; explains per-module units, compile-order dependence of the `timescale` directive, tool-specific defaults, and `timeunit`/`timeprecision`. Weak: says `$time` reports in the precision unit, or that `#1.55` delays exactly 1.55 ns.
questions.model_answer:
The time unit (1 ns) scales delay values; the time precision (100 ps) is the resolution delays are rounded to (§3.14.2, §22.7).

- `#1.55` is 1.55 ns, rounded to the precision: 1.6 ns. `set` becomes 0 at 1.6 ns. The second delay also rounds to 1.6 ns, so `set` becomes 1 at 3.2 ns.

- `$time` returns an integer in the module's time unit, rounded: 2 after the first delay and 3 after the second. The precision does not affect that rounding (§20.3.1).

- `$realtime` returns a real in the module's time unit: 1.60 and 3.20 (§20.3.3).

So the printed `$time` values (2, 3) do not match when things happened (1.6 ns, 3.2 ns). The LRM's own example with `timescale 10 ns / 1 ns` shows the same effect (§20.3.1).

Two modules can disagree because each module uses its own unit and precision. `#1` in a 1 ns module and `#1` in a 1 ps module are 1000× apart, and the same `#1.55` rounds differently under different precisions. Worse, the `timescale` directive applies to every following design element until the next one, so compile order can change a module's time unit. If nothing in the compilation sets a time unit, the default unit and precision are tool-specific (§22.7, §3.14.2.3). Mixing is not allowed, though: it is an error for some design elements to have a time unit and precision while others have none (§3.14.2.3). Prefer `timeunit`/`timeprecision` inside each module or package, which take precedence over the `timescale` directive (§3.14.2.3).
follow_ups: What does `$printtimescale` report and why is it useful in a mixed-vendor IP integration?
What is `#1step` in terms of time precision?
A VIP compiled with `1ps/1ps` drives a DUT compiled with `1ns/1ns`. What can go wrong with `#1` delays in the VIP?
common_mistakes: Assuming `$time` is in the precision unit.
Relying on a `timescale` directive in another file through compile order.
Assuming fractional delays are kept exactly.

questions.prompt: Walk through the simulation regions of one time slot in order. Where do concurrent assertions sample their values, and where do they evaluate? Can a region run more than once in a time slot?
questions.rubric: Strong: all nine regions in order including Re-Inactive; sampling in Preponed versus evaluation in Observed; program code in Reactive; clocking drives in Re-NBA; `$strobe`/`$monitor` in Postponed; states that the active and reactive sets iterate before time advances. Staff signal: PLI regions and what the LRM leaves nondeterministic within a region (§4.7). Weak: says assertions read this edge's post-NBA values, or lists eight regions with no notion of iteration.
questions.model_answer:
IEEE 1800-2023 defines nine simulation regions (§4.4.2):

1. Preponed: read-only; the values that concurrent assertions and default `#1step` clocking-block inputs use are the values here, before anything changes in the slot.

2. Active: module processes resume; blocking and continuous assignments update; nonblocking right-hand sides are evaluated.

3. Inactive: processes resumed after `#0`.

4. NBA: nonblocking updates from module code.

5. Observed: concurrent assertions (properties) are evaluated; clocking-block events `@(cb)` trigger here (§14.10).

6. Reactive: program-block code, checker blocking assignments, and assertion action blocks (§4.4.2.6).

7. Re-Inactive: `#0` inside the reactive set.

8. Re-NBA: nonblocking updates from program code and clocking-block drives (§14.16).

9. Postponed: read-only; `$strobe` and `$monitor` print here (§4.4.2.9).

Concurrent assertions evaluate in Observed using values sampled in Preponed (§16.5.1). So an assertion at a clock edge sees the register values from *before* that edge's NBA updates. That is the same value a flop would capture.

Iteration. The regions are not a single pass. When the reactive set creates new Active events (for example, a program writes a design signal), the reference algorithm goes back to Active and runs the active set again, so Observed can run more than once in a slot (§4.5, §14.13). Time advances only when every region is empty. Expert layer: there are also PLI regions (Pre-Active, Pre-NBA, Post-NBA and others) for VPI callbacks (§4.4.3).
follow_ups: A `$display` and a `$strobe` both print `q` right after `q <= d` at a clock edge. What does each print?
Why can a program block that writes a design signal cause Observed to run twice in one time slot?
Within the Active region, which execution order does the LRM guarantee, and which does it leave open?
common_mistakes: Saying concurrent assertions read values after the NBA updates of the current edge.
Forgetting Re-Inactive, or calling Re-NBA part of the Reactive region; it is a separate region of the reactive set.
Treating the list as one pass, so the loop back to Active is never mentioned.

questions.prompt: A testbench drives `valid` with a blocking assignment at `@(posedge clk)`. On simulator A the DUT captures it at edge 2; on simulator B at edge 3. The trace below shows what each simulator captured. Explain why the two runs differ, and how a clocking block removes the race.
questions.code:
```text
TB code:  @(posedge clk); valid = 1;      // driven at edge 2

edge          1    2    3    4
clk           /    /    /    /
valid (TB)    0    1    1    1           // written in Active at edge 2
dut.v_q  A    0    1    1    1           // DUT process ran after TB
dut.v_q  B    0    0    1    1           // DUT process ran before TB
```
questions.rubric: Strong: identifies the blocking TB drive at the active edge as the race and names §4.7 ordering freedom; explains both traces; gives the clocking-block fix with drive timing (Re-NBA), input sampling (#1step = previous Postponed value, equal to Preponed) and `@(cb)` timing (Observed). Weak: "add `#1`" or "use `#0`" as the fix; claims the drive lands in the NBA region; or says inputs are read after this edge's NBA updates.
follow_ups: What changes if the input skew is an explicit `#0`? When is the value read, and what is the risk?
Why is `#0` before the drive not a real fix?
With a `default clocking`, what does `##2` do, and why is it a compile error without one?
common_mistakes: Fixing the race with `#1` delays or `#0`. That moves the race, it does not remove it.
Saying clocking-block drives land in the NBA region or depend on the caller's region; zero-skew drives mature in Re-NBA (§14.16).
Blaming one simulator as buggy. Both orders are legal.

questions.prompt: What does a `program` block change about scheduling and about how the simulation ends? Why do most UVM testbenches start the test from a module instead? Where does a `final` procedure fit?
questions.rubric: Strong: Reactive/Re-NBA scheduling; what a program may not contain; thread-kill and implicit `$finish` rules; why UVM prefers a module top with clocking blocks; programs not deprecated; `final` runs at end of simulation with no timing controls. Weak: "programs are deprecated", or claims program code runs before the design in the same time slot, or places `final` inside the time-slot regions.
questions.model_answer:
A program block is a scope for testbench code (§24.3):

- Its `initial` procedures and blocking assignments run in the Reactive region, after the design's Active and NBA activity and after concurrent assertions are evaluated in Observed; its nonblocking assignments mature in Re-NBA (§4.4.2.6, §4.4.2.8). That was designed to separate testbench and design activity in the same time slot (§24.4).

- It may contain declarations, classes, subroutines and `initial`/`final` procedures, but not `always` procedures, module instances, interfaces or other programs (§24.3).

- When all `initial` procedures of a program finish, the program kills its remaining descendant threads. When every program's `initial` threads have finished, the simulator calls `$finish` implicitly (§24.3).

Why UVM benches use modules. UVM runs its phases in threads forked by `run_test()`, and components fork long-lived threads of their own. If `run_test()` sits in a program, the program's end-of-`initial` rules interact with those threads: ending the program kills descendants and can end the whole simulation, so phase and objection control is no longer the only thing deciding when the test stops. Clocking blocks already give the race-free sampling and driving that programs were designed for, so modern benches use a module top, class-based components, and clocking blocks in interfaces. Programs are not deprecated; they are just rarely needed.

`final` procedures run once at the end of simulation, after time stops (§9.2.3). They behave like functions: no delays, no waits. Use them for last-chance reports, such as closing files or printing summary counters. They are not part of any time-slot region.
follow_ups: A clocking block is declared in a program and the clocking event is generated by the program. What race does §14.13 warn about?
What runs first at the end of simulation: UVM's report phase or a `final` block? Why?
Can a program call a task defined in a module? Can a module call into a program?
common_mistakes: Calling program blocks deprecated.
Forking background threads inside a program and being surprised when they are killed at the end of `initial`.
Putting delays or event controls in a `final` procedure.

questions.prompt: Both packages below pull in the same file with the `include` directive. Why does the assignment in `top` fail to compile, even though the class text is identical? What is the rule for sharing types across packages?
questions.rubric: Strong: explains textual include creates two declarations and cites the matching-types rule; fixes with declare-once/import-elsewhere; mentions compile order and the limits of include guards. Weak: blames a missing include guard, or says identical class text gives one type.
questions.model_answer:
The `include` directive is textual substitution, so each package declares its own class named `txn`. A class typedef matches only itself within the scope where it is declared (§6.22.1, rule d), so `agent_a_pkg::txn` and `agent_b_pkg::txn` are different types that happen to have the same name and body. Assigning one to the other is illegal, `$cast` between them fails, and a factory override registered for one never applies to the other.

Rule: declare each shared type once, in one package, and `import` it everywhere else:

```systemverilog
package txn_pkg;
  `include "txn.svh"           // the only place txn is declared
endpackage

package agent_a_pkg;
  import txn_pkg::*;
  // agent code uses txn_pkg::txn
endpackage
```

Related rules:

- A package must be compiled before any code that imports it (§26.3).

- Importing a package does not re-export what *it* imported; use `export` if a package should pass names through (§26.6).

- Two wildcard imports that both provide a name are legal until code refers to that name; then the reference is an error (§26.5, Table 26-1).

- Include guards (an `ifndef TXN_SVH` / `define TXN_SVH` pair) stop a file being included twice in one compilation unit; they do not prevent this bug across packages.
follow_ups: Why would an include guard not fix this?
What is `$unit`, and why should shared testbench code avoid declaring things there?
How does this bug show up in UVM at run time if it slips through compilation?
common_mistakes: Treating the `include` directive like an import.
Believing include guards protect against duplicate types across packages.

questions.rubric: Strong: compilable interface with parameter, ports and three modports; correct connection; explains modport as a direction view with no storage and that driving an input is an error; mentions clocking blocks and virtual interfaces. questions.prompt: Why do class-based testbenches use virtual interfaces? What happens at run time if the driver uses its virtual interface before anyone has set it?
questions.rubric: Strong: static instance vs dynamic objects; virtual interface as a reference; null use is a fatal run-time error; type includes parameters and modport; access through the clocking block; config_db as the hand-off. Weak: "it's a pointer to the DUT" with no static/dynamic reasoning, or claims a missing virtual interface is caught at elaboration.
questions.model_answer:
An interface instance is part of the static hierarchy: it is created at elaboration, in a module. Class objects are created at run time and cannot have ports. A virtual interface is a variable that holds a reference to an interface instance, so class code can read and drive that instance's signals (§25.9). The top module instantiates the interface, connects it to the DUT and hands the reference to the classes; in UVM that hand-off goes through `uvm_config_db`.

Details that matter in practice:

- A virtual interface is null until assigned, and using a null virtual interface is a fatal run-time error (§25.9). The usual cause is a `config_db` get that silently failed, so check the get and fail loudly in `build_phase`.

- The type includes the interface's parameters (and modport, if one is selected). `virtual bus_if #(32)` and `virtual bus_if #(64)` are different types (§25.9). In UVM this has a second consequence: `uvm_config_db#(T)` is parameterized by the stored type (IEEE 1800.2-2020 C.4.2), and its `get` looks the entry up by that type as well as by scope and name, so a `get` with a different virtual interface type does not find the `set`. That lookup rule is UVM behaviour, not an IEEE 1800 rule.

- Drive and sample through the clocking block (`vif.cb.valid <= 1`, `@(vif.cb)`) so the class code is race-free (§25.9.1, Clause 14).

- One class can be pointed at different instances at different times, which is what makes agents reusable.
follow_ups: Your `config_db::get` returned 0. List three reasons a set and a get can fail to match.
Why might you give the driver a modport-qualified virtual interface type?
How would you share one virtual interface type across a parameterized family of agents?
common_mistakes: Expecting a null virtual interface to be caught at compile or elaboration time. It fails only when used, at run time.
Setting with `uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)` (the default `W = 32`) and getting with `uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if #(64))`: different types, so the get returns 0.
Driving `vif.valid` directly at `@(posedge vif.clk)`, which reintroduces the TB/DUT race.
sources: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_config_db_implementation.svh (get looks up by uvm_resource#(T) type)

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a module and a class in SystemVerilog? Why can a class-based driver not simply declare ports to reach the DUT?
questions.rubric: Strong: static elaborated hierarchy vs run-time objects reached through handles; predicts `42` and explains handle copying; names what a class cannot contain and links that to virtual interfaces. Weak: "modules are for design, classes are for testbenches" with no lifetime or handle explanation, or claims `p2 = p1` copies the object.
questions.model_answer:
A module is static structure. It is elaborated once before simulation starts, has ports, and contains `always`, `initial` and continuous assignments and instances of other modules. Its hierarchy never changes at run time, and a synthesizable subset of modules describes hardware (Clause 23).

A class is a data type. Objects are created at run time with `new` and are reached only through handles. Classes support inheritance, virtual methods and constrained randomization, and an object is reclaimed automatically once no handle refers to it (Clause 8, §8.29).

Handle semantics are the first trap: `p2 = p1` copies the handle, not the object, so the code prints `42` (§8.12). A second object needs `new` (or a copy method).

A class cannot contain ports, `always` or `initial` procedures, continuous assignments or module instances. Its objects come and go during simulation, while signals belong to the static hierarchy. So class code reaches DUT signals through a virtual interface: a variable that holds a reference to a static interface instance (§25.9). The top module creates the interface, connects it to the DUT and passes the handle to the classes.
follow_ups: How would you make `p2` an independent copy? What does `p2 = new p1;` copy, and what does it not copy?
When is an object's memory freed, and what keeps it alive?
Can a class be declared inside a module? What changes if it is declared in a package instead?
common_mistakes: Saying assignment copies the object. It copies the handle; both names refer to one object.
Saying classes "cannot be synthesized, so they cannot touch signals". The real reason is that class objects are dynamic and have no ports; the bridge is a virtual interface.

questions.prompt: Predict each line's output or say why it does not compile. Then explain when you need `$cast` and what happens when it fails.
questions.rubric: Strong: handle-type binding for non-virtual methods and properties, object-type dispatch for virtual methods, both compile errors with reasons, function-form `$cast` success and failure; links virtual dispatch to factory overrides. Weak: predicts `derived::who` for (1) or `2` for (3), or says `$cast` throws an error when used as a function.
questions.model_answer:
1. `base::who x=1`. `who` is not virtual, so the call is bound by the handle type (`base`), and `base::who` reads `base::x`.

2. `derived::vwho`. A virtual method dispatches on the object type: the call runs the most-derived override for the object's actual class, here `derived` (§8.20).

3. 1. Properties are never virtual. `derived::x` hides `base::x`, and a `base` handle sees `base::x`.

4. Compile error. `extra` is not a member of `base`; the compiler checks names against the handle type.

5. Compile error. Assigning a superclass handle to a subclass variable is illegal without a cast (§8.16).

6. Prints `extra`. `b` refers to a `derived` object, so the dynamic cast succeeds (§8.16, §6.24.2).

7. Prints `cast failed`. `b` now refers to a plain `base` object, which is not a `derived`. Called as a function, `$cast` returns 0 and leaves `d2` unchanged; called as a task, a failed cast is a run-time error (§6.24.2).

When you need `$cast`: any time you move from a general handle to a specific one: a factory `create` returning a base type, `clone()` returning `uvm_object`, items arriving through a generic port. Always use the function form and check the result, so a wrong type gives your message instead of a null-handle crash later.

Why it matters in UVM: factory overrides only work because the test calls methods through base-class handles and those methods are virtual. A non-virtual method in a base class silently ignores the override.
follow_ups: A base-class constructor calls a virtual method that the derived class overrides. Which version runs, and what state will it see?
Once a method is declared virtual, can a subclass make its override non-virtual?
What is `super.vwho()` for, and when must a derived constructor call `super.new()`?
common_mistakes: Expecting properties to behave virtually.
Using the task form of `$cast` or ignoring the function's return value.
Forgetting `virtual` on a base method, so overrides through base handles never run.

questions.prompt: Predict the two lines the `initial` block prints. Then say whether each commented-out part, (3), (4) and (6), would compile if you uncommented it. Explain the order in which a derived object is constructed, and the difference between `local` and `protected`.
questions.rubric: Strong: predicts `len=4` and `size=12 tag=2` from the order base initializers, base constructor body, derived initializers, derived constructor body; rejects (3) because `local` members are invisible in subclasses, (4) because the compiler-inserted `super.new()` has no value for `id`, and (6) because `protected` members are invisible outside the class and its subclasses; knows `super.new` must be the first statement and that its arguments are evaluated before the derived class's initializers run. Weak: predicts `size=11`, says a missing `super.new` skips the base constructor, or treats `local` and `protected` as the same.
questions.model_answer:
Construction order (§8.7, §8.17). The first action of `child::new` is `super.new(7)`, and the chain runs root first:

- In `base::new`, the properties of `base` are initialized first: `m_len = 4`, `tag = 1`, and `m_id` takes its uninitialized value. Then the body runs: `m_id = 7`, `tag = 2`.

- When `super.new` returns, the properties of `child` are initialized: `size = tag + 10` reads the `tag` that the base body already set, so `size` is 12.

- Then the rest of `child::new` runs.

So the output is:

```text
len=4
size=12 tag=2
```

The commented-out parts:

- (3) Does not compile. `m_id` is `local`: it is visible only inside methods of `base` and is not visible in subclasses (§8.18). A non-local method of `base` that uses `m_id` still works when inherited.

- (4) Does not compile. `orphan::new` has no `super.new` call, so the compiler inserts `super.new()` with no arguments (§8.15, §8.17). `base::new` has no default for `id`, and leaving out an argument that has no default is a compile error (§13.5.3). Fixes: call `super.new(0)` as the first statement; or write the constant in the `extends` clause, `class orphan extends base(0);`, in which case the constructor must not call `super.new` itself (§8.17); or, in IEEE 1800-2023, declare `function new(default);`, which copies the base constructor's argument list (§8.17). Giving `id` a default also compiles, but then every subclass that forgets `super.new` silently passes that default.

- (6) Does not compile. `m_len` is `protected`: like `local`, it is hidden from code outside the class, but unlike `local` it is visible in subclasses, which is why (2) is legal (§8.18).

Two related traps:

- `super.new(...)` must be the first statement executed in the constructor (§8.15, §8.17), and its arguments are evaluated before the derived class's initializers run. `super.new(size)` would pass an undefined value, because a property's value before its initialization is undefined (§8.7).

- A virtual method called from `base::new` runs the `child` override before the `child` properties are initialized (§8.17 NOTE 2).

A constructor may itself be `local` or `protected` (§8.7), for example to force creation through a static method. A `local` constructor makes the class impossible to extend, because a subclass cannot call `super.new` (§8.17 NOTE 1).
follow_ups: Why must every UVM component constructor call `super.new(name, parent)`, and what breaks if it passes the wrong `parent`?
When would you give a class a `protected` constructor, and how would code outside the class create an object of it?
What does `function new(default);` in a derived class expand to, and when is it clearer than writing the arguments out? (§8.17)
common_mistakes: Expecting the compiler to skip the base constructor when `super.new` is missing; it inserts `super.new()` with no arguments.
Giving the base argument a default to silence the error, so every subclass that forgets `super.new` silently passes the default.
Making members that extensions need `local`, so subclasses cannot reach them; use `protected` for those.

questions.prompt: Predict what the last line prints. Then write a deep `copy` method and explain how the same mistake shows up in a monitor-to-scoreboard path.
questions.rubric: Strong: predicts 4 and 2 and explains handle copying for nested objects (§8.12); writes a correct deep copy that allocates nested objects and handles null; makes it virtual for polymorphic cloning; connects to the reused-monitor-object bug and the analysis-port handle semantics. Weak: predicts 1 for `h.id`, or writes a "deep copy" that assigns `copy.h = h`.
follow_ups: What state does `new p1` copy besides properties? (Hint: RNG state and `rand_mode`/`constraint_mode`, §8.12.)
Why is calling `new` inside `copy()` of a base class a problem for derived classes, and how does UVM's `create`/`do_copy` split solve it?
When is sharing a sub-object on purpose the right choice?

Writing a non-virtual `copy` that slices derived objects into base objects.
Reusing one transaction object in a monitor.

questions.prompt: The base and derived versions of a virtual method have different default argument values. A call through a base handle omits the argument. Which delay value does the derived body receive?
questions.rubric: Strong: separates which body runs (certain, derived) from which default is used (not specified by the LRM); cites §8.20's presence-only rule and §13.5.3; labels any specific answer as tool behaviour; gives the fix and the interface-class rule. Weak: answers confidently with 10 ("like C++") or 1 ("because it is virtual") as if it were a language rule, or claims the code does not compile.
questions.model_answer:
The body that runs is certain: `send` is virtual, so `drv_fast::send` executes (§8.20). The default value is not pinned down by IEEE 1800-2023:

- §8.20 requires only that the presence of a default match between the virtual method and its override: "It is not necessary to have matching default expressions". So the code is legal.

- §13.5.3 says a default is evaluated in the scope containing the subroutine declaration, each time a call uses it, but does not say which declaration (the handle type's or the object type's) supplies the default for a virtual call.

So whether this prints `fast delay=10` or `fast delay=1` is not specified. A simulator may follow the C++ rule (the static type's default, giving 10), but that is that tool's choice, not a SystemVerilog rule. A portable testbench must not depend on it.

What to do: treat differing defaults on virtual overrides as a bug. Keep every override's default identical to the base, or remove the default and pass the argument explicitly. For interface classes the LRM is stricter: a method default must be a constant expression with the same value in every class that implements it (§8.26.8).
follow_ups: What must match between a virtual method and its override (§8.20)? List four things.
How would you write a lint rule that catches this?
What does the `:initial` or `:extends` method specifier in IEEE 1800-2023 protect against?
common_mistakes: Importing the C++ rule and stating it as SystemVerilog fact.
Thinking different default expressions are a compile error.

questions.prompt: Predict both printed counts. Then explain how the same rule makes the UVM factory's type registration work.
questions.rubric: Strong: predicts 3 and 1; explains per-specialization statics and that the default specialization matches `#(int)`; connects to `uvm_*_registry` singletons; suggests a non-parameterized base for shared state. Weak: predicts 4 (one shared static) or treats `counter` without parameters as a distinct type from `counter #(int)`.
questions.model_answer:
It prints `3 1`.

A parameterized class is not a type; each specialization (the generic class plus a set of parameter values) is a separate type, and each specialization has its own copy of every static member (§8.25). `counter #(int)`, the typedef `cnt_int` and the default `counter` (T defaults to `int`) are all the same specialization, so `a`, `b` and `d` increment one counter: 3. `counter #(byte)` is a different type with its own `count`: 1. To share a static across specializations, put it in a non-parameterized base class (§8.25).

UVM factory link. The `uvm_component_utils(my_comp)` macro declares `typedef uvm_component_registry #(my_comp, "my_comp") type_id;`. `uvm_component_registry #(T, Tname)` has a `static function get()` holding a `static` instance, so every registered class gets its own singleton proxy, created once per specialization (uvm-core 2020.3.1 `uvm_registry.svh`). That proxy registers with the factory and later builds objects of exactly type `T` when the factory asks. One generic class, a distinct singleton per registered type: that is this rule at work.

Practical corollaries:

- A parameterized agent with two widths has two sets of statics (instance counters, shared config caches), which surprises people who expected one.

- Two specializations are different types, so a handle of one cannot hold the other; share behaviour through a common non-parameterized base class or an interface class.

- Use `typedef` for each specialization you use, so every file names it the same way.
follow_ups: Two modules each declare the same parameterized class locally. Are `C #(8)` in module A and `C #(8)` in module B the same type? (§8.25 on declaration context.)
How do you call a static method of a specialization without creating an object?
Why does the `uvm_component_param_utils` macro register without a type name, and what does that prevent?

Two classes hold handles to each other. How do you make them compile? (Forward-declare the second with `typedef class C2;` before the first; its full declaration must follow in the same scope, §8.27.)
common_mistakes: Expecting one static shared by every specialization.
Passing handles between specializations that "look the same".

questions.prompt: You are designing the API for a reusable VIP so that users can plug in their own reference models and response checkers. When would you use an abstract base class (`virtual class` with `pure virtual` methods) and when an interface class? Show both.
questions.rubric: Strong: correct rules for both (constructability, contents, single extends vs multiple implements); compilable sketches; a design rationale tied to UVM's fixed base classes; mentions casting between interface-class and class handles. Weak: treats interface classes as SystemVerilog `interface` constructs, or says abstract classes cannot have implemented methods.
follow_ups: Two interface classes declare a method with the same name and different signatures. What happens when one class implements both (§8.26.6)?
Can an interface class be parameterized? What would you use that for?
Why can a UVM component not simply extend your abstract VIP base?
